questions.prompt: A bug reproduces only against a Docker service running on your laptop, and the fix depends on changes you have not committed. Where should the agent run?
options: A cloud session, because it can clone the branch and run the service in its sandbox
A local session on your machine, because that is the only surface that can see your uncommitted changes and reach the running service
A Slack `@Claude` mention, because it starts a task from team chat
A scheduled task, because it will retry until it succeeds
questions.explanation: Both constraints are local: uncommitted work exists only in your working tree, and a service bound to your machine is not reachable from a cloud clone. A local session (CLI or Desktop) is the surface that has both. A is tempting because a cloud sandbox sounds more capable, but it clones the repository — it never sees your uncommitted edits — and it is a different machine than the one running your Docker service. C starts a fresh cloud session, inheriting the same two blind spots. D changes when it runs, not what it can see.

questions.prompt: You want a CI failure to be acted on in the same session where you are currently debugging, with your files open. Which mechanism fits?
options: A Slack `@Claude` mention in the channel where CI posts
A channel that pushes the CI event into your open session
A cloud session triggered on the failing pipeline
questions.explanation: A channel is an MCP server that pushes an event into the session already running, which is exactly 'act on this where my files already are.' A Slack mention is the tempting near-miss: it starts a *fresh cloud session* on a clone, so it loses your open context. A cloud session on the pipeline has the same problem plus a different checkout. Remote Control lets you drive a session from another device; it does not inject an external event, so there is nothing for CI to trigger.

questions.prompt: You plan to leave a channel running overnight so CI failures get handled while you sleep with your terminal closed. What is wrong with that plan?
options: Nothing — the channel keeps a process alive after the session ends
A channel only delivers events while its session is open, so you need a persistent or background session, not a closed terminal
Channels work overnight but only for messages from the allowlisted sender
Channels run in the cloud, so closing the terminal is fine
questions.explanation: A channel pushes into a *running* session. Close the session and there is nowhere for the event to land — the receive end is gone, which is the same mistake as expecting a cross-session message to arrive after the tab is closed. To get always-on behaviour you keep a session alive in a background process or a persistent terminal. A is the exact misconception to kill. C names a real gate (the allowlist) but not the reason the plan fails. D is false: channels deliver to your machine's local session, not to a cloud host.
